definitions.text: A woman; a girl. Also 'my girlfriend': ma meuf.

examples.text: Il est venu avec sa meuf.
Y a une meuf qui te cherche.
examples.translation: There's a woman looking for you.

origin.etymology: Verlan for femme: fe-mme reversed to me-fe, then compressed to meuf. One of the oldest and most fully naturalised verlan words — it appears in dictionaries and many speakers no longer register it as reversed at all.

definitions.text: A guy, a bloke. Also 'my boyfriend': mon keum.

examples.text: C'est qui ce keum?
Son keum bosse dans la restauration.

origin.etymology: Verlan for mec ('bloke'), which is itself informal. Verlan frequently takes slang as its input rather than standard vocabulary, producing a second layer of concealment.

definitions.text: A guy, a bloke. The everyday word for an unnamed man.
Used to address a friend: 'mec, arrête' — 'mate, stop'.
A boyfriend: mon mec.

examples.text: Ce mec est vraiment sympa.
Mec, tu déconnes.

pronunciation.respelling: GAH — the r and s are silent

definitions.text: A guy; a lad. Slightly softer and more rural-sounding than mec. Les gars addresses a group.

examples.text: Salut les gars, ça va?
C'est un bon gars.

definitions.text: A mate, a pal. Warmer than copain and used of close friends.

examples.text: Je sors avec des potes ce soir.
examples.translation: I'm going out with some mates tonight.

examples.text: C'est mon pote depuis le lycée.
examples.translation: He's been my mate since secondary school.

definitions.text: Bro; brother. An address term between male friends, very common in youth speech.

examples.text: Ça va, frérot?
Merci frérot, t'es le meilleur.

definitions.text: The French practice of inverting a word's syllables to create a slang form. Not a single word but a whole productive system, and the single most distinctive feature of French slang.

examples.text: Meuf, keum et relou, c'est du verlan.
examples.translation: Meuf, keum and relou are all verlan.

examples.text: Les jeunes inventent du verlan tous les jours.
examples.translation: Young people coin new verlan constantly.

origin.etymology: The name is itself verlan: l'envers ('the reverse') becomes verlan. Some words have been reversed twice — beur, verlan for arabe, was re-reversed into rebeu once beur became mainstream. That double inversion is a defence mechanism: verlan exists to stay ahead of outsiders.
origin.firstAttested: documented from the 19th century; widespread from the 1970s

definitions.text: Annoying, tiresome, heavy going. Of people and of situations alike.

examples.text: Il est trop relou avec ses questions.
examples.translation: He's so annoying with all his questions.

examples.text: C'est relou de devoir y retourner.
examples.translation: It's a pain having to go back there.

origin.etymology: Verlan for lourd, 'heavy' — which in French already means 'tiresome' when applied to a person.

definitions.text: Shady, weird, off. Of people, places and situations that don't feel right.

examples.text: Ce mec est un peu chelou.
examples.translation: That guy is a bit shady.

examples.text: C'était une ambiance chelou.

origin.etymology: Verlan for louche, which already means 'shady'. As with relou, the verlan form has largely displaced the original in casual speech.

definitions.text: Shady, suspicious, dubious. The standard-register word that chelou reverses.

examples.text: Cette affaire est louche.
examples.translation: There's something dodgy about this business.

examples.text: Un quartier un peu louche la nuit.
examples.translation: A slightly dodgy neighbourhood at night.

definitions.text: Hey; yo. A greeting, and also an attention-getter: wesh, tu fais quoi?
Used alone as an expression of surprise or indignation.

examples.text: Wesh, ça va ou quoi?
Wesh, t'as vu ça?

origin.etymology: From Algerian Arabic wešnu / weš rak, 'how are you'. One of many Maghrebi borrowings that entered French through the banlieues and then spread nationally through rap. It is strongly marked — using it outside its home register sounds like an imitation.

definitions.text: To love, to really enjoy. Je kiffe ce morceau — 'I love this track'.
To fancy someone: je la kiffe grave.

examples.text: Je kiffe trop cette série.
Il la kiffe depuis la rentrée.
examples.translation: He's had a thing for her since term started.

origin.etymology: From Arabic kayf, 'pleasure, state of wellbeing' — the same root as the English word kif. Arrived through Maghrebi French and is now thoroughly mainstream, used comfortably by speakers of every background.

definitions.text: Bitterness, rage, the sting of a defeat. Avoir le seum is to be gutted and furious at once — there is no single English word for it.

examples.text: J'ai le seum, on a perdu en finale.
examples.translation: I'm sick about it, we lost in the final.

examples.text: Ça lui a mis le seum.

origin.etymology: From Arabic sèmm, 'poison'. The metaphor is exact: bitterness as something toxic you have swallowed.

definitions.text: Gutted, bitterly disappointed. Nothing to do with revulsion in this use — it is the French equivalent of British 'gutted'.

examples.text: Je suis dégoûté, j'ai raté le train.
examples.translation: I'm gutted, I missed the train.

examples.text: Il était trop dégoûté après le match.
examples.translation: He was absolutely crushed after the match.

definitions.text: Very, really. An intensifier: c'est grave bien, 'it's really good'.
Standing alone: totally, absolutely. An emphatic agreement.

examples.text: C'était grave bien, ce concert.
—Il exagère, non? —Grave.

definitions.text: Really, so. In informal speech trop has lost its sense of excess and simply intensifies: c'est trop bien means 'it's brilliant', not 'it's too good'.

examples.text: Elle est trop sympa, ta sœur.
J'ai trop envie d'y aller.

definitions.text: Completely, downright, absolutely.
Alone as a reply: definitely; too right.

examples.text: Il a carrément oublié de venir.
—On y va? —Carrément.

definitions.text: Meh. Signals indifference or a lukewarm opinion, and is a complete answer on its own.

examples.text: —Tu as aimé le film? —Bof.
Bof, je préfère rester ici.

origin.etymology: A conventionalised sound rather than a word, usually accompanied by a shrug and a downturned mouth. Together with the shrug it is one of the most recognisable gestures in French conversation.

definitions.text: Anyway; in short. Used to cut a digression short and get back to the point, or to end a story that has run out of road.

examples.text: Bref, on n'est jamais arrivés.
Bref, tu vois le genre.
examples.translation: In short, you get the idea.

definitions.text: So; therefore; as a result. Nominally causal, in practice an all-purpose connector used several times a sentence by many speakers.

examples.text: Il pleuvait, du coup on est restés.
examples.translation: It was raining, so we stayed.

examples.text: Du coup, tu viens ou pas?
examples.translation: So are you coming or not?

origin.etymology: Its explosive spread since the 2000s is one of the most complained-about changes in contemporary French. Language columnists have been objecting for two decades with no discernible effect.

definitions.text: Like. A quotative and approximator, precisely parallel to English 'like': il a fait genre 'je sais pas'.
Faire genre: to put on an act, to pretend.

examples.text: Il m'a dit, genre, qu'il avait oublié.
examples.translation: He told me, like, that he'd forgotten.

examples.text: Arrête de faire genre.

definitions.text: There you go; that's it. Handing something over, or confirming that someone has understood.
Used to close a statement when there is nothing more to add — often trailing off: et voilà, quoi.

examples.text: Voilà, c'est fait.
Il est parti, et voilà.

definitions.text: A sentence-final particle with no translatable content, roughly the function of 'you know' or 'innit' — it marks the statement as obvious or already shared.

examples.text: C'est pas compliqué, quoi.
Il est sympa mais bizarre, quoi.
examples.translation: He's nice but odd, if you see what I mean.

definitions.text: Work; a job. Métro, boulot, dodo — 'commute, work, sleep' — is the standard French summary of a dreary routine.

examples.text: Je pars au boulot dans dix minutes.
examples.translation: I'm leaving for work in ten minutes.

examples.text: Il a trouvé un boulot à Lyon.
examples.translation: He's found a job in Lyon.

definitions.text: To work, especially to work hard. Bosser dur is to graft.

examples.text: Elle bosse dans une agence de com.
examples.translation: She works at a communications agency.

examples.text: J'ai bossé tout le week-end.

definitions.text: To laze about, to do nothing in particular. A glandeur is a layabout.

examples.text: J'ai glandé tout l'après-midi.
Qu'est-ce que tu glandes?
examples.translation: What on earth are you doing?
examples.context: In a question it means 'what are you messing about at', and it is impatient.

definitions.text: Money, cash.

examples.text: J'ai plus de thune jusqu'à la fin du mois.
examples.translation: I'm out of money until the end of the month.

examples.text: Ça coûte une thune, ce truc.

origin.etymology: Originally a five-franc coin in 19th-century argot. The coin is long gone; the word outlived it, as money slang usually does.

definitions.text: Money. One of several French food-words for cash, alongside oseille (sorrel) and fric.

examples.text: Il se fait du blé avec ça.
examples.translation: He's making good money out of that.

examples.text: Faut du blé pour habiter Paris.
examples.translation: You need money to live in Paris.

origin.etymology: Grain as a metaphor for wealth is nearly universal — English dough, Spanish pasta, Italian grana. Agricultural staples become the measure of value in slang everywhere.

definitions.text: Broke, skint. Often intensified: fauché comme les blés — 'broke as the wheat fields', i.e. cut down to nothing.

examples.text: Je suis fauché, on fait ça chez moi.
examples.translation: I'm broke, let's do it at my place.

examples.text: Étudiant et fauché, le classique.
examples.translation: A skint student, the classic combination.

definitions.text: A nightmare; a real struggle. Quelle galère! — 'what a palaver'.
As a verb, galérer: to struggle, to have a hard time of it.

examples.text: Trouver un appart à Paris, quelle galère.
examples.translation: Finding a flat in Paris is a nightmare.

examples.text: Je galère avec ce logiciel.

origin.etymology: From the galley ships rowed by convicts — a sentence to the galleys was the harshest punishment short of death. Molière's 'que diable allait-il faire dans cette galère?' kept the image alive.

definitions.text: A thing; a whatsit. The universal placeholder for an object whose name escapes you.
A trick or knack: il y a un truc pour l'ouvrir.
Something that is or isn't one's cup of tea: c'est pas mon truc.

examples.text: Passe-moi le truc là, sur la table.
examples.translation: Pass me that thingy on the table.

examples.text: La danse, c'est pas mon truc.

definitions.text: A thingamajig; also a person whose name you've forgotten. Monsieur Machin is the French 'Mr Whatsisname'.

examples.text: Où est le machin pour ouvrir les bouteilles?
examples.translation: Where's the thingy for opening bottles?

examples.text: J'ai croisé machin, tu sais, du bureau.
examples.translation: I ran into whatsisname, you know, from the office.

definitions.text: A gadget or doohickey — a placeholder for a small object, usually one with a mechanism.

examples.text: C'est quoi ce bidule sur l'étagère?
examples.translation: What's that gizmo on the shelf?

examples.text: Il a acheté un bidule pour la cuisine.
examples.translation: He's bought some gadget for the kitchen.

definitions.text: To eat — bluntly and without ceremony. La bouffe is the noun: grub, food.

examples.text: On va bouffer un truc?
examples.translation: Shall we go grab something to eat?

examples.text: La bouffe était excellente.

definitions.text: Pre-dinner drinks with something to nibble. A social institution rather than a meal, and prendre l'apéro is an invitation in itself.

examples.text: On se fait un apéro vers sept heures?
examples.translation: Shall we have drinks around seven?

examples.text: Apéro chez nous samedi, viens.
examples.translation: Drinks at ours on Saturday, come along.

origin.etymology: Clipped from apéritif. The French pattern of clipping the end of a word — apéro, resto, ado, dico, ordi — parallels Australian -o words and is just as productive.

definitions.text: To drink alcohol, usually to excess. Implies a habit rather than an occasion.

examples.text: Il picole trop depuis quelque temps.
examples.translation: He's been drinking too much lately.

examples.text: On a picolé jusqu'à trois heures.

definitions.text: Drunk. The everyday word for it, and not especially crude.
Of a place: crammed full. Le métro était bourré.

examples.text: Il était complètement bourré hier soir.
examples.translation: He was completely hammered last night.

examples.text: Le bar était bourré à craquer.
examples.translation: The bar was packed to bursting.

definitions.text: A hangover. The image is of a mouth so dry it might be carved from wood.

examples.text: J'ai une gueule de bois carabinée.
Gueule de bois assurée demain matin.

definitions.text: A party. Verlan for fête.

examples.text: Il y a une teuf chez Sarah samedi.
examples.translation: There's a party at Sarah's on Saturday.

examples.text: C'était une bonne teuf.

definitions.text: Crazy, mad, incredible. Verlan for fou. Un truc de ouf is 'something insane', usually admiringly.
Separately, as an interjection: phew, the sound of relief. The two are unrelated and distinguished by position.

examples.text: C'est un truc de ouf, ce concert.
Ouf, j'ai cru que j'avais perdu mon passeport.
examples.translation: Phew, I thought I'd lost my passport.

definitions.text: Rubbish, useless, hopeless. Of things: c'est nul. Of people: je suis nul en maths, 'I'm useless at maths'.

examples.text: Le film était vraiment nul.
Je suis nul en cuisine.

definitions.text: Rubbish; broken; knackered. Of objects that no longer work and of people who are exhausted.

examples.text: Mon vélo est naze.
Je suis naze, je vais me coucher.
examples.translation: I'm shattered, I'm going to bed.

definitions.text: To exasperate; to wear someone down with talk. Tu me soûles — 'you're doing my head in'.

examples.text: Il me soûle avec ses histoires.
examples.translation: He's doing my head in with his stories.

examples.text: Ça me soûle de devoir recommencer.
examples.translation: It's exhausting having to start over.

definitions.text: Trouble; a falling-out; a messy situation. Chercher les embrouilles is to go looking for a fight.

examples.text: Je veux pas d'embrouilles.
Il y a eu une embrouille à la sortie du bar.
examples.translation: There was a row outside the bar.

definitions.text: To mess about; to talk nonsense. Tu déconnes? — 'are you kidding?'
Of a device: to play up. Mon ordi déconne.
Sans déconner: seriously, no joke.

examples.text: Sans déconner, il a vraiment dit ça?
Ma connexion déconne depuis ce matin.
examples.translation: My connection has been playing up since this morning.

origin.etymology: Built on a vulgar root, though the word itself is widely used and lands closer to 'to mess about' than to anything stronger.

definitions.text: Damn; bloody hell. The most common French expletive, expressing anything from awe to fury.
As an intensifier before a noun: putain de voiture, 'bloody car'.
In the south, and especially Marseille, putain functions as near-continuous punctuation with almost no force at all.
definitions.note: Its literal meaning is a slur for a sex worker, which is worth knowing even though almost no speaker intends it.

examples.text: Putain, il fait froid!
Putain de bordel, où sont mes clés?
examples.translation: For God's sake, where are my keys?

definitions.text: Damn; shit. General-purpose frustration.
Good luck — said to a performer before going on stage, exactly as English says 'break a leg'. Replying merci is thought to break the charm.

examples.text: Merde, j'ai oublié mon portefeuille.
Merde pour ton concours demain!
examples.translation: Good luck with your exam tomorrow!
examples.context: Entirely sincere and kindly meant. The theatre origin is a horse-drawn-carriage superstition: more manure outside meant a bigger audience.

definitions.text: That works; okay; sounds good. Agreement to a plan, and the standard confirmation from a waiter taking your order.

examples.text: —On dit vingt heures? —Ça marche.
Deux cafés, ça marche.

definitions.text: Deeply annoying; boring to the point of pain. Stronger than relou and rather cruder.

examples.text: Cette réunion est chiante.
T'es vraiment chiant, tu sais.
examples.translation: You're really irritating, you know that.

definitions.text: Atmosphere, vibe. Used far more often in French than the borrowed English word is in English — il y a de l'ambiance means a place is buzzing, and 'bonne ambiance' is high praise for an evening.

examples.text: Il y avait une super ambiance hier.
examples.translation: There was a great atmosphere yesterday.

examples.text: Ambiance de merde à la réunion.

definitions.text: Nice, lovely, great. Gently dated — warm, a little old-fashioned, and the sort of word a grandparent uses approvingly.

examples.text: C'est chouette, ce petit café.
Chouette, tu es venu!

definitions.text: Nice, friendly, pleasant. Of people above all, but also of places and plans. One of the most-used adjectives in spoken French.

examples.text: Ta collègue est très sympa.
C'est sympa comme quartier.

origin.etymology: Clipped from sympathique. The clipping is so complete that the full form now sounds stiff in speech.

definitions.text: Having had enough; being fed up to the back teeth. J'en ai ras-le-bol — 'I've had it up to here'. The noun is also used in political commentary for public exasperation.

examples.text: J'en ai ras-le-bol de cette situation.
examples.translation: I've had more than enough of this situation.

examples.text: Un ras-le-bol général chez les employés.

origin.etymology: The image is of a bowl filled right to the brim — one more drop and it overflows. English reaches for the same picture in 'the last straw'.

definitions.text: Fair point; you're not wrong. Grudging agreement, often from someone who did not want to concede the point.

examples.text: —Ce serait moins cher en train. —C'est pas faux.
C'est pas faux, mais quand même.

origin.etymology: Given a second life by the television series Kaamelott, where a character uses it to conceal that he has not understood a word. Many French speakers now use it with that joke in mind.
